articles.title_orig: NASA opens recruitment for its next generation of astronauts
articles.title_zh: NASA opens recruitment for its next generation of astronauts
articles.content_orig:
The NASA logo is seen at NASA's Johnson Space Center, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, in Houston. Karen Warren/AP hide caption
If you have dreams of going to the moon, you now have a chance. NASA is accepting applications for those interested in becoming an astronaut.
The candidates selected to be astronauts would not only test spacecraft but would also live and work on the moon in a future moon base, said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in a statement released on Saturday.
"Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage," the statement said. "NASA's astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation."
There are currently 32 active astronauts in NASA's astronaut corps. Since NASA missions began in the 1960s, the agency has selected 370 people to train as astronauts, according to the agency.
The applicant process is extremely competitive. Out of more than 8,000 applicants for NASA's last astronaut class, only 10 candidates were selected.
While any U.S. citizen can apply and there is no official age restriction, applicants will need to have a master's degree in a STEM-related field such as engineering or math.
In a recent change, a nursing degree qualifies.
"Nursing degrees are now included in the STEM definition," Anna Schneider, NASA spokesperson, told NPR on Sunday. "Master's-level nursing degrees now meet the minimum educational requirement, whereas nursing degrees were previously excluded."
In addition, NASA is requiring a minimum of three years of related professional experience after completing a degree.
In lieu of a master's degree and working experience, NASA will consider those in a PhD program (in STEM), doctors or pilots with extensive flight experience.
FILE - This detail of a July 20, 1969 photo made available by NASA shows astronaut Neil Armstrong reflected in the helmet visor of Buzz Aldrin on the surface of the moon. Neil Armstrong/NASA via AP hide caption
If chosen, the selected astronauts will undergo training that will last for two years. NASA said astronauts will prepare for critical and difficult missions such as landing near the moon's South Pole.
To achieve its goal of returning humans to the moon in 2028 – the first time since 1972 – NASA is relying on private companies such as Blue Origin and SpaceX to develop systems and spacecraft.
During a Nov. 7 press conference on the Artemis III moon mission's progress, Isaacman said he is "very confident" the mission will launch in 2027.
The starting salary is $164,395 and applications will be received through Dec. 3.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Opens Investigation Into Jensen Huang’s Relationship With Chinese Spy
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Opens Investigation Into Jensen Huang’s Relationship With Chinese Spy
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia announced Sunday it is launching an independent investigation into its chief executive and founder, Jensen Huang, over concerns he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
The statement, published on the company’s website, comes after US officials have expressed concern over Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company. (The two are not related.)
Separately, Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair in a note to staff, though he did not name the other person in the affair.
The Financial Times previously reported that US intelligence provided information to US officials that the two were in a romantic relationship, according to unnamed people familiar with a memo on the intelligence, the FT reported. Nvidia is the world’s leading chipmaker amid the AI boom and has a market capitalization of about $4.5 trillion.
The company previously said in a statement that Jensen Huang’s meetings were “not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” It added that any concerns about illegal chip diversion were “debunked last year.”
Nvidia said a committee of independent directors and outside counsel will oversee its investigation.
“The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. But, the board “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”
“Today’s news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption,” a spokesperson for Nvidia told CNN.
Huang, 63, said that he was “unfaithful” and hurt his wife and children in the note to Nvidia staff.
“I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it,” Huang said, adding that he supports Nvidia’s investigation. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security.”
President Donald Trump said Sunday that he has not spoken to Huang after Nvidia announced the investigation , but that he “probably has an excuse for it.”
“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” Trump told reporters as he left Florida.
Trump also mused that he “probably has an excuse for it.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to reporters Sunday in Florida, declined to comment on the Nvidia situation.
On Thursday, Republican chairmen of three influential House panels — the committees on Foreign Affairs, the Chinese Communist Party and Intelligence — said in a news release that they sent a letter to Huang “requesting that he appear before their committees for a joint, closed-door briefing on Huang’s interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, a publicly reported People’s Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset, and NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage.”
“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.”
In a note, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville & Ives Co., called the news “a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons.”
“The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?” he said.
Ives also said the investigation “would increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China.”
This story has been updated with additional content.
CNN’s Logan Schiciano and Molly English contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures rise slightly as investors eye AI trade, brace for more data and earnings: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures rise slightly as investors eye AI trade, brace for more data and earnings: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures were slightly higher Sunday evening with traders eyeing whether technology shares can continue to recover, while they are awaiting the release of key inflation data and earnings from major AI companies this week.
S&P 500 futures gained 0.1%, while the Nasdaq 100 's added 0.3%. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 101 points, or 0.2%. Over in Asia, markets were mixed on Monday, with Japanese equities leading the rise. The Nikkei 225 gained 2.5% and the Topix climbed 2.97%.
South Korea's benchmark Kospi index rose 0.66%, after initially starting in negative territory, while the small-cap Kosdaq index declined 0.81%.
Tech heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix were up 1.64% and 2.03% respectively.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.51%.
Later Monday, investors will look to inflation data out of China, with economists polled by Reuters expecting a reading of 0.8%, down slightly from September's 0.9%.
Friday's market partially rebounded from Thursday's brutal AI-driven selloff, as chip stocks recovered on renewed buying. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite bounced 1.09% to 24,579.42 and the broad-market S&P 500 rose 0.31% to 7,376.86. The blue-chip Dow , however, lost 237.33 points, or 0.46%, to settle at 51,285.73.
Broader investor sentiment remained cautious following a batch of stronger-than-expected jobs data. Additionally, concerns linger after the Democrats' strong midterm results, amid fears that tighter regulations on data center construction, energy use, and development costs could slow the AI infrastructure boom.
The tech sector will also be focused on the bombshell announcement Sunday that Nvidia's board of directors is opening an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. A proxy for Nvidia shares was lower by 2% over the last 24 hours in trading on Hyperliquid.
Liz Ann Sonders, Schwab Center for Financial Research chief investment strategist, noted that the Nasdaq and Nasdaq-100 are oversold, with heavy de-risking by traders. Thursday marked the biggest day of retail selling since the Covid pandemic, according to Vanda Research. Retail traders haven't been taking advantage of the selloff, Sonders said.
"Retail has not proven to be the dip buyers that they have been in the past," she told CNBC's "Fast Money" on Friday. "You saw a really heavy amount of net selling … we may not fully be washed out yet, but we'll have to see whether that retail trader at some point decides to step back in."
Sonders suggested that the next short-term focus should be on companies' adjustments to capex plans and expectations for future profit margins.
This week , investors are looking ahead to key AI-related earnings — CoreWeave, Cisco and Applied Materials are all on deck — as they assess the outlook for tech and whether the recent selloff has further to run.
They'll also watch for the releases of both the consumer price index on Tuesday and the producer price index on Friday, looking for clues on the Fed's next move.
On Monday, traders will get September wholesale inventories data at 10 a.m. ET. Take-Two Interactive Software, Occidental Petroleum, KKR, Constellation Energy and Skydance are scheduled to report quarterly earnings.
Asia-Pacific markets mostly fell on Monday, with South Korean equities continuing their sharp sell-off from Friday.
The benchmark Kospi index fell 0.69%, while the small-cap Kosdaq index declined 0.87%.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.31%, after initially starting the day in positive territory.
The only outlier in the region was Japan, which saw the Nikkei 225 gain 1.44% and the Topix climb 2.09%.
Asia-Pacific markets look stronger to start the week after last week's tech sell-off.
Futures for Japan's Nikkei 225 in Chicago were at 58,520, while in Osaka they were last at 58,250 compared with the index's previous close of 57,434.77.
Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index last traded at 24,647, compared with the index's last close of 24,481.86.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.2% in early trading.
Later Monday, investors will also look to inflation data out of China, with economists polled by Reuters expecting a reading of 0.8%, down slightly from September's 0.9%.
Nvidia has opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.
Huang told Nvidia staff in an email on Sunday that he had an affair with the woman and that Nvidia's board of directors had opened an independent investigation into the spying allegations.
An Nvidia spokesperson said that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption.
Read Huang's email to Nvidia employees and the company board of directors' statement here .
— Kif Leswing, Kamaron McNair
Stock futures fell to begin trading Sunday night.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 93 points, or 0.2%. S&P 500 futures slid 0.4% and Nasdaq 100 futures tumbled 0.8%.

articles.title_orig: Rubio Warned Officials About Nvidia Chief’s Entanglement With Chinese Spy
articles.title_zh: Rubio Warned Officials About Nvidia Chief’s Entanglement With Chinese Spy
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers his keynote on the company's GTC event in Berlin, Germany, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Markus Schreiber/AP hide caption
The massive artificial intelligence chip maker Nvidia says it is launching an internal investigation, after reports that the company's CEO was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
In the statement announcing the investigation, Nvidia cited recent reporting by The New York Times , which alleges Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation that sought to send advanced Nvidia AI chips to China.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the statement from the company's board of directors reads in part.
The Times released a series of reports over the last two weeks detailing Huang's alleged relationship with a woman named Alice Huang, who is accused of being a spy for China. The two are not related. NPR has reached out to the Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C. but has not received a response.
"Alice Huang is a Chinese national. She's a Chinese businesswoman who had something of a mysterious and meteoric rise," Times reporter Ana Swanson explained on NPR's technology podcast Machine Gods .
Alice Huang ran a Singapore-based company that purchased nearly $5 billion in Nvidia chip technology, Swanson says. "At the same time, she was also seen personally with Jensen Huang on a couple of occasions after some industry events in Taiwan. They were photographed together both at a bar with other suppliers and then also out to dinner with some other executives."
The reporting by the Times suggests Alice Huang may have helped China get around U.S. limits on exports of powerful AI chips.
According to Nvidia, Huang sent an email to his employees on Sunday, acknowledging the relationship, and apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife.
"I support the investigation and will cooperate fully," Huang wrote. "I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."
Last week, three Republican members of Congress sent a letter to the Nvidia CEO requesting that he brief lawmakers about the relationship, and about the company's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage."
Nvidia dominates the global market for AI chips, and has seen explosive growth in recent years, as NPR has reported . The company started as a manufacturer of chips for computer graphics, which later turned out to be crucial for training artificial intelligence .
Nvidia's CEO and President Trump have repeatedly appeared in public together in recent years. According to Huang, Nvidia is helping to fund the construction of a new ballroom at the White House.

articles.title_orig: A Missionary Pope Faces a Chain Saw-Wielding Populist in Argentina
articles.title_zh: A Missionary Pope Faces a Chain Saw-Wielding Populist in Argentina
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has called on Argentine President Javier Milei and the country’s political leaders to “safeguard democracy” and demonstrate a “careful use of words” during his first speech in Buenos Aires.
The American pope arrived in Argentina on Sunday, embarking on a trip that his predecessor, the first Argentine pope, was never able to make.
Leo’s highly anticipated papal visit to Argentina began with a private meeting with President Milei shortly after the pope landed. Milei has received strong backing from US President Donald Trump, with whom Leo, first American pontiff, has publicly disagreed, particularly on the treatment of migrants and the war in Iran.
The pope’s visit comes at a time when Milei’s “chainsaw” austerity measures have led to welfare spending cuts. Milei has also equated state-led social justice programs with communism and has also been accused of undermining democracy through attacks on the press and divisive rhetoric. He has also struggled to secure bipartisan agreements.
“Democracy, then, is also a part of Argentina’s heritage that needs to be safeguarded,” the pope said at a meeting with politicians, members of civic society and the diplomatic corps at the Palacio Libertad. “Democracy is also strengthened by the daily conduct of public life: through willingness to listen, through careful use of words, through the patient search for agreement, and through the ability to see those who think differently as fellow citizens with whom we share a common future.”
The Chicago-born pontiff, who recently cast a mail-in ballot during the US mid-term elections, talked about the importance of the “freedom to elect one’s own leaders through the ballot box.” He urged leaders to recognize the limits of their power, and said that democracy is protected by “confidence in the law”, the ability to freely express convictions and for institutions to serve all parties.
“Authority is most authentic when it is exercised as service, when it looks beyond the immediate, and when it uses its power to promote the welfare of all,” the pope said. An eruption of applause from the audience forced him to repeat his next line: “Those who exercise authority have a duty to act with prudence, to acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them.”
Leo’s November 8-11 trip is the first papal visit to Argentina in almost four decades and it comes with the added dimension that Pope Francis did not make a return trip home during his 12-year-papacy. Millions are expected to attend the various services and events while the pope is in the country.
Francis’ decision not to visit Argentina was something even his closest friends were unable to explain. Some have suggested the late pope’s reluctance to visit was linked to Argentina’s polarized political culture, with Francis wary that his presence in the country could be weaponized.
The Argentine pope had a strong emphasis on the church helping the most marginalized in society. Francis lamented Argentina’s economic decline which he blamed on decades of bad governance. He contrasted the roughly 5% inflation rate he recalled from his youth with the soaring inflation and high poverty rates of recent years.
In his speech, Leo cited Argentina’s “abundance of human resources” but called for its “wealth bear fruit for the benefit of all and warned that corruption undermines trust in institutions.
Before his election as pope in 2013, Francis served as archbishop of Buenos Aires, where he spoke out on social justice and was unafraid to criticize political leaders.
Leo’s visit, the second leg of his 12-day tour of South America, will underline the ways he continues the reforms of his predecessor, but with his own distinctive style.
Pope Leo, in contrast, has made the church’s social teaching and concern for the marginalized a central concern of his papacy. His itinerary in Argentina includes a visit to a federal prison in Buenos Aires and a stop at a care center for people with intellectual and physical disabilities in Claypole which has been affected by the Milei cuts.
During his presidential campaign and in the years leading up to it, Milei repeatedly insulted Francis, calling him an “imbecile” for defending social justice, “the representative of the evil one on earth” and a “sh*t of a pope.” Milei later apologized for these remarks and called Francis “the most important Argentine in history” following the pontiff’s death in April 2025, repeating the compliment in his remarks on Sunday.
Milei and Francis met in the Vatican in February 2024, with the pope joking with the president: “you cut your hair!” — a reference to the unruly hairstyle which earned Milei the nickname “The Wig.” Milei replied that he had “tidied it up.”
Leo and Milei previously met at the Vatican in June 2025. After meeting Milei in the Casa Rosada on his arrival in Buenos Aires, the pope was presented with the keys to the city of the Argentine capital by the mayor, Jorge Macri.
CNN’s Claudia Rebaza contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: 10 takeaways from Trump's 60 Minutes interview: Why GOP lost the midterms, what went wrong on immigration and more
articles.title_zh: 10 takeaways from Trump's 60 Minutes interview: Why GOP lost the midterms, what went wrong on immigration and more
articles.content_orig:
Days after Republicans faced a series of bruising midterm election losses, President Trump stood by his handling of the economy and the Iran war — but he acknowledged some "bad messaging" on economic issues and said his immigration crackdown was "too tough" at times.
In a sitdown with 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat, the president also suggested some top administration officials could be on their way out. One hour later, he announced White House chief of staff Susie Wiles would depart her role and be replaced by Stephen Miller.
Here are the biggest takeaways from the interview:
Republicans lost more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats on Tuesday, with some races still uncalled, including in places that Mr. Trump won by double-digit margins two years ago. About 63% of midterm voters disapproved of Mr. Trump's job performance, and 44% said one reason for their vote was to express opposition to him, according to CBS News exit polling.
Asked for his analysis of the midterm losses, Mr. Trump told 60 Minutes that voters "didn't like the war" with Iran or the soaring gas prices that it triggered.
But he said he believes the primary reason for Republicans' losses was that "I was not on the ballot," an explanation he has offered several times in recent days. He suggested his pre-election endorsements and rallies "brought a lot of people … a lot closer to victory."
Ahead of Election Day, the president frequently urged his supporters to "pretend that I'm on the ballot." So, what happened?
"I think they didn't vote, really. I think they didn't vote. I think in some cases, they didn't like the candidates. And that's, you know, their prerogative," he said.
Some of the candidates were picked by the president. He endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Lone Star State's bitter GOP Senate primary, and he endorsed Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill her late brother's South Carolina Senate seat — encouraging her to run for a full term.
Mr. Trump argued that "Cornyn would have lost also."
The president defended his stewardship of the economy in his 60 Minutes sitdown, which came hours after a stronger-than-expected jobs report . He said "the numbers are phenomenal."
"We're doing numbers that have never been done before. 401(k)s are at their all-time high by a lot. Under other presidents, they were a disaster. 401(k)s have made people rich," the president said. Pressed on the fact that not all Americans have large retirement accounts, Mr. Trump responded: "But a lot of people do."
But exit polling shows three-fourths of midterm voters viewed the condition of the economy as either poor or not so good — and 70% of that group voted for Democratic House candidates. Voters were especially concerned about prices of gasoline, food, utilities and healthcare, and two-thirds of voters believed that Mr. Trump's tariff policies hurt the country's economy.
Mr. Trump said the problem is that "we couldn't get the word across."
"I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me, but I would talk about it all the time. So I don't know, how much can I talk about it?" the president said.
He predicted that Americans are "going to notice it in the next two, three, four months," arguing that his policies will lead to a resurgence of manufacturing jobs.
The morning after the election, Vice President JD Vance argued on social media "the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone" — the broadly unpopular Iran war."
Mr. Trump said Vance told him about his plan to write that post, and he responded: "You write what you want." The president said "I don't disagree" with the vice president's diagnosis for why the Republicans lost the midterms, "other than one thing."
"The one thing he left out is — that I would say, and maybe he wouldn't say it, I don't know. I've never asked him really. But, if you had … to do again, would you do it? And that's Iran. Would you go and attack Iran?" he said.
The president said his answer to that question is an "emphatic yes," arguing Iran's conventional military has been degraded and its nuclear program has been set back.
"I think historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not? But … I have to go with what's right for our country," he said. "If they had a nuclear weapon during my term, I would be excoriated far worse than what's happened."
In a visit to the Oval Office later in the day, Mr. Trump reiterated his view that historians will judge the Iran war more favorably than voters. He pointed out a portrait of Ulysses S. Grant, a former president whose reputation has improved with age .
"I mean, he was very low on the list and now he's much higher on the list," Mr. Trump said. "I think as an example — the fact that I have taken the nuclear weapon away from Iran will not be good, short-term. But long-term, I think it's going to be very important."
Since September, Iran and the U.S. have largely held off from major attacks, though the U.S. launched a set of limited defensive strikes on Iranian targets earlier this week.
Mr. Trump has suggested in recent months that the war could ramp up again after the election, but he has also frequently predicted Iran is interested in striking a deal, and Qatar is mediating a diplomatic push between the two sides. He told 60 Minutes he believes Iran is close to striking a deal, but the outcome of the election "gives them a little bit of a hope certificate."
Asked if he plans to escalate the war now that the midterms are over, the president said: "Well, I'm not looking to. I don't think there's any reason to."
Mr. Trump's victory in 2024 was fueled in part by voters' discontent with the Biden administration's immigration policies. But this year, exit polling shows 58% think the Trump administration's actions on immigration have gone too far. In battlegrounds like Texas, many Latino voters who shifted to Mr. Trump two years ago pivoted back to Democrats due to concerns about immigration policy .
The president said immigration "both helped and hurt."
"I think I got an A+ for closing up the border," he said.
So, which immigration policies hurt him?
"For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," Mr. Trump said. "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally."
He continued: "Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."
"I think it was too tough," the president said of his deportation policies.
Mr. Trump's plans for the second half of his term aren't clear. On Friday, he replaced White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, a hardliner who is widely viewed as an architect of the Trump administration's immigration enforcement strategy. Last year, he pressed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to conduct at least 3,000 arrests per day .
The president said he'd "love to do something on immigration" with congressional Democrats.
Mr. Trump is the wealthiest person to hold the presidency, and his wealth has grown by billions in recent years, fueled partly by his family's cryptocurrency ventures . Polls show many voters believe the president is prioritizing his personal business interests while in office.
Asked about reporting by Forbes that his net worth has soared since he returned to the White House, Mr. Trump said, "So did everyone." (Douthat noted that, unlike Mr. Trump, his net worth hasn't gone up by nearly $3 billion. The president responded, "Well, you should've had stock.")

articles.title_orig: Oil falls on open as Trump says fresh Iran attacks 'unlikely'
articles.title_zh: Oil falls on open as Trump says fresh Iran attacks 'unlikely'
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices on Friday posted a steep weekly loss, as investors weighed the risk of renewed military escalation between the U.S. and Iran following the midterm elections.
International benchmark Brent crude futures added 3 cents to close at $98.32 per barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 31 cents to settle at $90.83 per barrel. Brent fell more than 16% for the week while U.S. crude lost neary 13%.
Investors are assessing whether the conclusion of the U.S. midterm elections could pave the way for renewed actions against Iran, potentially threatening oil supplies from the Middle East.
Bob McNally, Rapidan Energy Group founder and president, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" that he sees an 80% probability of military fighting resuming, forecasting that both oil benchmarks could climb above $100 a barrel.
However, hopes for a diplomatic resolution have also emerged after Iran reportedly sent a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar, Reuters reported, citing a senior Iranian official.
Iran reported three additional attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, while data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) indicated that attacks on vessels were continuing at a near-record rate.
"President Donald Trump is determined, as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally said.
"The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it. And as long as that core difference in that deal space is absent, the escalation dynamic remains in place," he added.
McNally's view is shared by other analysts, including Lombard Odier's chief economist Samy Chaar and head of investment strategy Luca Bindelli.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s proposed Russia deal raises NATO alarm as ex-commander warns Putin seeks influence over Europe
articles.title_zh: Trump’s proposed Russia deal raises NATO alarm as ex-commander warns Putin seeks influence over Europe
articles.content_orig:
Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove warns any deal meeting Russia's demands could face European resistance.
President Donald Trump's push for a deal with Russia to end the war in Ukraine and potentially reshape European security has raised alarm among NATO allies, with a former top alliance commander warning Fox News Digital that President Vladimir Putin has long sought to divide the world into competing spheres of influence.
The warning came as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also appeared to reject what he called a potential "Yalta 2.0," and NATO allies debated direct outreach to Putin ahead of delegations preparing for talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11.
Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove , the former Supreme Allied Commander Europe, warned that Putin's ambitions extend far beyond Ukraine and reflect a broader vision for how global powers should divide influence.
"Putin has a plan for the world, and he has pushed that plan on leaders several times," Breedlove warned before adding: "He talks about it and he writes about it."
ZELENSKYY TO SEEK OFFRAMP FOR YEARS-LONG RUSSIA WAR IN UN SPEECH AFTER TRUMP REVEALS PEACE DEAL IS CLOSE
Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, front row from left, and Jonas Gahr Støre, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Ursula von der Leyen, Dutch Prime Minister Dick Schoof, and Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, back row from left, stand together in the chancellery in Berlin, Germany, on Dec. 15, 2025. (Markus Schreiber, Pool/AP)
Trump had suggested Thursday that an agreement with Moscow could extend beyond ending Russia's nearly five-year war in Ukraine.
"It's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine... I could even say it might involve all of Europe," Trump told reporters after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House.
"It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled," Trump added.
Breedlove said Putin has repeatedly promoted a vision of dividing global power among Russia, China and the United States.
"The plan is three spheres of influence whereby China controls the Far East, Russia controls Europe, and America controls the Western Hemisphere. I do not expect there's going to be a lot of cooperation from the countries of Europe," he said.
"The Western world is waiting to see what this big plan is, and they are very concerned because it is about them," Breedlove added.
President Donald Trump (R) and Russian President Vladimir Putin (L) hold a meeting at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Zelenskyy also warned Friday against repeating the 1945 Yalta Conference , where Allied leaders negotiated Europe's postwar order before the Soviet Union consolidated control over Eastern Europe.
"We don't want to have Yalta 2.0," the Ukrainian leader told CNN . "We don't want to be divided by Russia," he said before adding: "For me, it's not simple and it can be dangerous."
On Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that discussions on how Europe would look after the Ukraine war were already underway.
"It's one of the key topics that's been raised repeatedly in every conversation, anytime negotiations have been discussed," he said ahead of traveling to Paris for the G7 meeting.
RUBIO SOUNDS CAMPAIGN-READY AS HE RAILS AGAINST OPEN BORDERS, GLOBALISM IN SPEECH FROM ANCIENT GREEK RUINS
Secretary of State Marco Rubio talks to reporters at NATO Headquarters in Brussels, Belgium, on Friday, April 4. (Jacquelyn Martin/Pool/AP)
"So I think that's what the president is alluding to, is that there's been some advances made and what that architecture could look like post-conflict. We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point," he added, clarifying Trump's comments.
Breedlove, however, questioned whether European governments and Ukraine would even accept a broader agreement negotiated without their involvement.
"I do expect that when we get a peek under the hood of what Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump have devised that there may be European partners and allies to include Ukraine that may or may not be enthralled with the proposed solution."
"We have always said nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," the expert said.
"Neither have we heard anything about the EU or NATO being in this conversation. And yet the EU, NATO and Ukraine are central and the heart of the matter that apparently is going to be discussed."
Tensions also appeared to mount further after Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a rare 90-minute telephone conversation with Putin on Oct. 27, according to reports .
TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR
A composite image shows Russian President Vladimir Putin (L) and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (R) as peace talks continue. (Valery Sharifulin/Pool/AFP via Getty Images; Sean Gallup/Getty Images)
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized the separate European diplomatic initiatives.
"I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," she said as Breedlove went on to defend the outreach.
"The two calls that recently took place between Northern leaders in the NATO alliance and Russia, I don't think that they're out of place at all," he said. "I think they're entirely appropriate."
"The great powers of Europe are getting very concerned that someone is dealing with their security without including them in the conversation," he added.
Meanwhile, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot confirmed Sunday that France would participate in the Abu Dhabi negotiations.
"The Europeans will be well represented; France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in these discussions," Barrot said, according to Reuters.

President Donald Trump speaks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, as they meet to negotiate for an end to the war in Ukraine, at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, U.S., August 15, 2025. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)
Breedlove warned that any agreement requiring European nations to sacrifice their security to satisfy Moscow would still face fierce resistance.
"If the maximalist demands of Russia remain intact and in order to find peace, all the rest of Europe has to give up its security, sacrifice its security, make itself more susceptible to Russian attack, then this is not going to go well," he said.
"Putin has never been a partner for peace in Ukraine. Putin is not now a partner for peace in Ukraine."
"The EU nations, the NATO nations, and Ukraine are not going to sign up to a plan that suggests that Russia will be able to once again amass its armies, march across borders and intervene in its neighbors' internal business."

"We need to understand that we are in a war. Mr. Putin is at war with the West," he warned.

articles.title_orig: "Forever cruise" arrested at Singapore port, court records show
articles.title_zh: "Forever cruise" arrested at Singapore port, court records show
articles.content_orig:
The Odyssey, the "forever cruise" that has been stranded in Southeast Asia after its owner struggled with financial problems , has been arrested in Singapore, according to court records obtained by CBS News.
A Singaporean law firm, Helmsman LLC, is listed as the arresting solicitor, but it is unclear whom the firm is representing. A source familiar with the matter tells CBS News that it is likely a fuel supplier.
The luxury cruise ship is currently being operated by its lender after its owner, Villa Vie Residences, couldn't keep up with payments.
Villa Vie owes one supplier in the area approximately $500,000, though it's unclear whether that supplier hired the law firm to solicit the arrest.
A ship arrest is a legal process in which a vessel can be detained or seized following a legal claim.
The journey of the MV Odyssey luxury cruise ship, launched in October 2024, came to a sudden end last month in Cambodia, where residents on the ship had just hours to disembark.
According to accounts from multiple sources familiar with the final weeks on board, these details included a scramble to find fuel while stuck at a port in Singapore, a rush by the crew to obtain provisions once food shipments had ended, and the temporary detainment of the ship in Hong Kong.
This story published first on CBS News at 6:24 p.m. on Nov. 8, 2026.

articles.title_orig: Targeted by U.S., Armed Group Strikes Back in Colombia
articles.title_zh: Targeted by U.S., Armed Group Strikes Back in Colombia
articles.content_orig:
A drone attack on a military base in northern Colombia has killed three soldiers and wounded at least 16, the country’s armed forces said.
The Colombian military said in a statement on Saturday that the attack hit a base in Santa Rosa del Sur, a small town in the foothills of the San Lucas mountain range. Authorities have not said who carried out the strike, the latest in a series of attacks on security forces as violence rises across rural parts of the country.
The area is rich in gold mines and has long been disputed by rebel armed groups including the Gulf Clan, the National Liberation Army (ELN) and smaller groups led by former members of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC).
Footage shared on social media showed clouds of smoke rising from the base after three explosions, and soldiers taking cover in shelters made of sandbags.
“Those who were behind this attack… will have nowhere to hide,” President Abelardo de la Espriella wrote on X. “Every attack against our soldiers strengthens our resolve to defend Colombia.”
Violence has intensified in several rural areas since de la Espriella, a conservative, took office in August.
The president cancelled peace talks with rebel groups and has taken a confrontational approach, including more air strikes, deploying more troops in some cities and creating joint task forces to defend strategic assets such as a pipeline that runs from the Caribbean coast to central Colombia.
De la Espriella’s government argues that armed groups used ceasefires granted by the previous government to consolidate their grip on rural areas, where they tax local businesses and profit from the drug trade.
Some groups have responded by stepping up attacks on the country’s armed forces.
Last week, a military base in Tolima province was targeted with missiles made from gas canisters. The attack killed four civilians, including a two-month-old baby.
Police in the border city of Cucuta have been attacked several times with remotely activated bombs.
State forces and illegal armed groups carried out 34 attacks with bombs or explosives in Colombia in the four weeks to October 16, a 9 percent increase on last year’s four-week average, according to ACLED, a group that monitors armed conflicts.
A 2016 peace deal with FARC led to the demobilisation of more than 14,000 fighters, but smaller groups have since fought over the rebels’ former territory.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia announces probe into CEO Huang amid reports China spied on him
articles.title_zh: Nvidia announces probe into CEO Huang amid reports China spied on him
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang "is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA," the company said.
Tech giant NVIDIA has announced an investigation of its CEO amid allegations that he was the subject of an intelligence-gathering effort by the Chinese.
"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," the company said in a statement Sunday, adding that a "committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."
Jensen "fully supports the review" and will cooperate with it, the NVIDIA statement further said.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," according to the statement.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement further said.
"The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team," according to the statement.
The New York Times reported late last month that Huang, who runs the world's largest computer chip manufacturer, was targeted by a Chinese espionage plot centered around a woman they identified as Alice Huang, a top executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials determined was funneling information to Beijing and had developed a "close relationship" with Jensen Huang.
The Chinese government has denied the allegations, calling them "baseless and purely slanderous smears against China."
Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment after the New York Times story broke.
"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected" and are part of Jensen Huang's job, an NVIDIA spokesperson told ABC News at the time.
However, NVIDIA on Sunday shared with ABC News an internal message Jensen Huang sent to employees, in which he said he was "unfaithful" to his wife.
"My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," the message said, in part. It did not name Alice Huang nor any other person.
Addressing NVIDIA staff, partners and shareholders, Huang went on to say "my responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence."
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," Huang's message said.
Following the New York Times report, congressional Republicans on the Select Committee on China sent a letter to Jensen Huang requesting that he appear for a closed-door briefing Nov. 18 concerning his relationship with Alice Huang.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the letter said, in part. It is not known if Huang will appear before the committee.
“Today’s news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," an NVIDIA spokesperson told ABC News Sunday.

articles.title_orig: Newport Beach fishermen find Royal Caribbean cruise ship employee treading water 20 miles off coast
articles.title_zh: Newport Beach fishermen find Royal Caribbean cruise ship employee treading water 20 miles off coast
articles.content_orig:
Man taken to hospital after falling off Royal Caribbean ship in Pacific Ocean, with Coast Guard investigating incident
A pianist for a Royal Caribbean cruise ship is expected to survive after two Newport Beach, California , fishermen discovered him treading water in the Pacific Ocean nearly 20 miles (32km) offshore on Friday.
The unidentified man was taken to the hospital after the rescue, according to the US Coast Guard, which is now investigating how he went overboard from the cruise ship.
Authorities believe the man may have been in the ocean for approximately nine hours before he was spotted by Sean Norton and Grant Garrett, who were returning from a fishing trip near Catalina Island.
The two fishermen had spent the morning fishing for marlin when their trip took an unexpected turn. By noon, they had pulled the stranded man from the water.
“I’m like, ‘Yeah, it’s a human being. Stop the boat; let’s get all of our lines in,” Garrett told CBS News , recalling the moment the boat’s captain first saw the man in the water.
The fishermen quickly worked together to bring the man onboard. Once the man regained his composure, Garrett said he identified himself as a pianist onboard Royal Caribbean’s 14-deck cruise ship, the Ovation of the Seas.
According to Norton, the rescued crew member had few words to describe what he had just experienced. “The only thing he said to me was, ‘Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,’” Norton said.
After the rescue, the fishing crew issued an emergency maritime call, prompting Newport Beach lifeguards to respond and provide assistance. Battalion chief Adam Yacenda said the man was found approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, according to CBS, or “pretty much in the middle of the ocean”.
Despite the extended time spent in the water, Norton believes unusually warm ocean temperatures may have played a significant role in the man’s survival.
“You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water’s 76 degrees,” Norton said. “A different year, no way he makes it.”
The circumstances surrounding the crew member’s fall from the cruise ship remain under investigation by the Coast Guard. Royal Caribbean Group acknowledged the incident and said it is assisting the employee following the ordeal.
In a statement to CBS, a company spokesperson said: “We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share.”

articles.title_orig: Europeans will join Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, French foreign minister says
articles.title_zh: Europeans will join Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, French foreign minister says
articles.content_orig:
A view through the destroyed walls of a kindergarten shows a large bomb crater and a damaged residential apartment building following a missile attack in Kyiv, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. Dan Bashakov/AP hide caption
European officials will turn up for the U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates this week, France's foreign minister said Sunday, days after the Kremlin had insisted there could be no role for European powers at the meeting.
"France will be there and will ensure that Europe's voice is heard," Jean-Noël Barrot told French radio. He did not say who would represent Paris, or whether French or other European officials would take part directly in negotiations, or simply observe.
The meetings, which are set to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, had previously been presented as a three-way session between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.
The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had earlier ruled out a European role, saying the trilateral format had already been agreed.
Talking to a Russian news channel on Friday, he accused European governments of failing to decide who speaks for them, while acknowledging that security talks would at some point require Europe's involvement.
On Thursday, President Trump met Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and said a coming agreement was "going to involve more than Ukraine," adding he could even say it "might involve all of Europe."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told CNN on Friday that he had not been given details of the agreement Trump had referenced, and warned: "For me, it's not simple, and it can be dangerous." He invoked the 1945 Yalta conference, where Allied leaders settled Europe's division without the involvement of several affected countries.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, right, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attend a press conference in Berlin, Germany, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Ebrahim Noroozi/AP hide caption
This will be the fourth round of talks between the two warring nations brokered by the Trump administration, and the first since those in Geneva this February. Earlier U.S.-brokered meetings have made little progress, and the chances of a breakthrough have been reduced as the Trump administration focused on its war with Iran.
Moscow confirmed it would return to the negotiating table only following a visit by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg in October. Those talks saw Putin announce the release of an American prisoner from a Russian jail — an apparent Kremlin gesture to President Trump's earlier lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Ukraine was vehemently opposed to the fuel sales — arguing they helped replenish Moscow's war chest.
Witkoff has said the agenda for these latest talks will include postwar security arrangements and de-escalation of the conflict and humanitarian issues, shortly after Melania Trump helped broker a limited ceasefire that allowed humanitarian aid to enter a town inside Russian-occupied Ukraine.
Russia's delegation will again be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a hardline Putin aide who has participated in most talks with Ukraine since the unsuccessful first set of discussions all the way back in March 2022.
For the first time, these talks will also include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, as well as Yury Zhigarlovsky, a deputy head of the General Staff's operations directorate, alongside military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.
This more senior lineup could indicate that Moscow is readier than before to address thorny political and military questions. But the U.S. think tankInstitute for the Study of War suggested some of those same Russian officials have in fact previously sought to slow down previous talks or push harder on Moscow's demands.
The gaps between the two countries remain substantial. Russia has demanded that Ukraine give up large parts of its territory and renounce NATO membership. Zelenskyy has repeatedly insisted any security commitments should be clearly spelled out, including who would act, and how, if Russia attacked again.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, right, interacts with people at the monument to merchant Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky, leaders of the struggle against foreign invaders in 1612, in Red Square in Moscow, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, during National Unity Day celebrations. Yuri Kochetkov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin hide caption
Some analysts expect little. In an op-ed for the Atlantic Council think tank, the former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine John Herbst argued that Putin had rejected every U.S. proposal Kyiv accepted and preferred participating in peace talks than pursuing actual peace. "Perhaps the only outcome of the talks," he wrote, "will be to agree to another round."
The meetings in the United Arab Emirates also follow Democrats' midterm victories, which Zelenskyy said could improve Ukraine's chances of more U.S. aid.
Russia, too, may be looking to push for the Trump administration's outlines of a Ukraine deal — before a Democratic-controlled Congress arrives come January.
Also hovering over the talks — the prospect of Trump, Xi, and Putin gathering for a trilateral meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China later this month. While details remain murky, all sides have confirmed discussions are underway.
And as officials travel to Abu Dhabi to talk peace, the war has raged on regardless.
Zelenskyy said Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at the Kyiv area overnight Saturday, with only four intercepted, accusing Moscow of treating diplomacy "as a form of aggression."
In southern Ukraine, the death toll from a guided-bomb strike Monday on an aid distribution site in Komyshuvakha rose to at least 55.

articles.title_orig: Train crash kills seven, injures dozens near Egypt’s Cairo city
articles.title_zh: Train crash kills seven, injures dozens near Egypt’s Cairo city
articles.content_orig:
At least seven people have been killed and more than 125 others injured in a train crash on the outskirts of Cairo in Egypt’s Giza province, according to the country’s Health Ministry.
A train travelling between Giza and Fayoum on Sunday ran into the back of another train on the Cairo-to-Aswan route, causing the latter to derail from its tracks onto a countryside road in the district of al-Ayyat, authorities said.
Emergency rescue teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, Egyptian National Railways said.
Authorities say more than 70 ambulances were involved in transport and evacuation operations at the scene of the crash, with casualties taken to nearby hospitals.
President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi said he was following the accident “with great concern”, and had directed authorities to conduct an urgent investigation to “hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent”.
Witnesses described chaotic rescue efforts after the collision, as villagers, first responders and railway workers scrambled to reach passengers trapped inside overturned carriages.
Abdel Wahed Mohamed, 31, who was sitting at a nearby cafe when the collision occurred, said the Aswan-bound train had stopped, when the Fayoum-bound train crashed into it.
“The train overturned at around 1:30 pm [11:30 GMT]. Six carriages overturned,” he said, adding that victims suffered a range of injuries, including head wounds and broken limbs.
Another witness, Ahmed Moussa, 25, said rescuers dug beneath one overturned carriage to reach trapped passengers.
“There were people piled on top of each other inside,” he said, adding that he saw two women among the dead.
Taha Abdel Tawab, 43, said he “saw a young man leaving the train carrying his dead father”.
Al-Ayyat district, where the collision happened, is also the site of Egypt’s worst-ever rail disaster .
In 2002, more than 370 people were killed when a fire swept through a train carrying holiday travellers south of Cairo. In 2009, multiple train crashes in the area killed dozens.
Egypt’s 110 million people depend heavily on rail transport, but the cross-country network – one of the largest in Africa – is in need of modernisation.
Over the past decade, Egypt has poured billions of dollars into updating its transport infrastructure, including new highways and high-speed rail lines, but has yet to overhaul much of its dated train services .

articles.title_orig: Crash Warnings Are Piling Up on Wall Street. Jack Bogle Had a 6-Word Rule for Exactly This. - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: Crash Warnings Are Piling Up on Wall Street. Jack Bogle Had a 6-Word Rule for Exactly This. - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
Four crash warnings in one weekend, a 4.4% drop and the worst week since April. Jack Bogle's rule for moments like this was six words long, and his second rule, your age in bonds with Social Security counted, tells a…
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Jack Bogle’s rule for a week like the one that just ended was six words long: "Don’t do something, just stand there." The founder of Vanguard, who launched the first index fund for ordinary investors in 1976 and died in 2019 at 89, said it on CNBC in January 2016 during a global sell-off, had written it in his 2007 book, and repeated the 6-word rule for the rest of his life.
It is worth hearing again this weekend. The S&P 500 finished Friday 6% below its October 6 record after a 4.4% drop on Thursday and its worst week since April, and the crash warnings arrived in a pile: by Sunday afternoon four separate pieces predicting a crash or a bursting bubble sat near the top of the most-read lists, beside a fifth calling Berkshire Hathaway’s record $377 billion of cash a warning. Those warnings are a sign of how nervous Wall Street has become after one bad week; they are opinions about what could come next, and none of their authors knows the date, and Bogle did not claim to. When he gave the rule in 2011, as MarketWatch later reported, he added that it was good only about 99% of the time.
So what should a 70-year-old with $1.5 million actually do? Bogle left two rules, and the second one matters as much as the first. Take a 70-year-old widow with $1,050,000 in an IRA that was her late husband’s 401(k), $450,000 in a brokerage account, $2,900 a month in Social Security and $90,000 a year of spending. Her husband set the accounts at 60% stocks in 2019, and the bull market since has carried them to 70%: $1,050,000 in stock index funds, $450,000 in bonds and cash. If that sounds like you, the numbers below are yours.
The first rule is about the sale you are tempted to make this week. A dollar in the S&P 500 fund at the October 2007 peak was worth 44 cents at the March 2009 low. Held through it, the same dollar was worth $4.70 on Friday, before counting a single dividend. The 2007 to 2009 fall took 56.5% off the index and 5.4 years to get back to the old high. The 2020 fall took 34.1% in five weeks and was back in six months. The 2022 fall took 25.4% and two years. Each recovered for the investor who stood there.
Standing there is easier when the money you spend this year is nowhere near the stocks. That is where the second rule comes in.
Bogle’s second rule was roughly your age in bonds. He added a part most people leave out. In his 2012 book The Clash of the Cultures he wrote that your asset allocation should count the value of any pension and Social Security you expect to receive as a bond-like component of your wealth, and in interviews he priced a new retiree’s check at about $300,000 to $350,000.
For the widow, the check is $34,800 a year. Priced as a 20-year bond at the 10-year Treasury’s 4.84%, it is worth $439,629. Her wealth with the check counted is $1,939,629. Seventy percent of that in bonds is $1,357,741. Take away the check, and $918,111 of bonds belong inside the portfolio, which leaves $581,889 for stocks, or 38.8%. Call it 40/60: $600,000 in stocks, $900,000 in bonds.
Taken literally, without the check, the rule says 30/70: $450,000 in stocks, $1,050,000 in bonds. Either way she is at 70/30, and by Bogle’s arithmetic she has held too much stock for her age since long before Thursday. If you are 70, the same four steps work for you: price your check, add it to your savings, take 70% of the total in bonds, and subtract the check.
Here is what the three mixes do to $1.5 million in each of the last three big falls, with the stock side taking the full index loss and the bond side flat.
Where she is now. A 2007-size fall takes $592,974 and leaves $907,026; her $450,000 of bonds covers 8.2 years of the $55,200 a year she draws beyond Social Security. At 40/60 the same fall takes $338,842 and leaves $1,161,158, and $900,000 of bonds covers 16.3 years.
The number that decides. The longest wait in the table was 5.4 years after 2007. At $55,200 a year that is $299,690 of spending she would need from the bond side while the stocks came back. She already has $450,000 there, so standing there was survivable for her even at 70/30. The move to 40/60 is about the size of the loss she would have to sit through, and whether you can sit through $592,974 is a different question from whether you can sit through $338,842.
The move is $450,000 from stocks to bonds, and where you make it decides what it costs. Inside the IRA it costs nothing: sell $450,000 of the stock fund and buy Treasuries, and the IRA goes from $780,000 of stock and $270,000 of bonds to $330,000 and $720,000. No tax is due on a trade inside an IRA.
The brokerage account is the wrong place. Its $270,000 of index fund has a $120,000 cost basis, so selling it realizes a $150,000 gain, $22,500 of federal tax at 15%, and it lifts her income that year from $90,000 to $240,000, far past the $109,000 line where a single filer’s Medicare premiums go up two years later. Leave the brokerage account alone.
Once the move is made, $900,000 in Treasuries at the 10-year’s 4.84% pays $43,560 a year. With her $34,800 of Social Security that is $78,360, or 87% of her $90,000 of spending, before she sells a share of anything. The $11,640 gap comes from the stock side in good years and from the cash in bad ones. Hold the bridge in Treasuries or CDs held to maturity; a bond fund can lose value too, as 2022 showed.
In a repeat of 2007 to 2009 her portfolio would fall to $1,161,158, and she would not need to sell a share for years.
The rule is a rule of thumb, and Bogle said so. Pricing the check as a 20-year bond is our assumption; higher rates or a shorter life make it worth less. Inflation raises the $90,000 over 20 years, and the stock side is what pays for that, which is the argument for 40/60 over 30/70. And selling stock after a 6% drop is also doing something. Bogle’s answer was that your allocation is set by your age and your spending, not by the headlines: if 40/60 was right on October 6, it is right now, you make the change once, and then you stand there.
Four crash warnings in one weekend are a reading of Wall Street’s nerves after its worst week since April, and no one knows which of them, if any, is right. Jack Bogle’s six words say not to sell into them. His second rule, your age in bonds with Social Security counted, says a 70-year-old widow with $1.5 million belongs near 40/60, not 70/30. Made inside the IRA, the move costs $0 in tax, cuts her loss in a 2007-size fall from $592,974 to $338,842, and leaves $900,000 of bonds paying $43,560 a year, which with her Social Security covers 87% of her spending while she waits.

articles.title_orig: Not McDonald's: The '40s Fast Food Chain Boomers Prefer Over The Rest
articles.title_zh: Not McDonald's: The '40s Fast Food Chain Boomers Prefer Over The Rest
articles.content_orig:
Being food nerds, we're always intrigued by the fast food preferences of different generations. For example, Gen Z and millennials have a higher tendency to hit the drive-thru when compared to other demographics. But we really like to get into overall food preferences, such as what people enjoy eating — and our elder generation, the baby boomers, have a fast food restaurant chain which they hold in higher regard than the rest. Surprisingly, it's not the easily accessible McDonald's, but rather, Dairy Queen.
According to a current YouGov survey of respondents' positive opinions of dining brands, the baby boomer cohort is particularly fond of the place that serves the fluffy soft serve with that signature curl on top. (It comes in second place after Baskin-Robbins, but we're comparing places that also serve hot food, which Dairy Queen does at most locations.) McDonald's, however, comes in at a shocking 43rd place in terms of positive opinions. Clearly, Dairy Queen, which was founded in Joliet, Illinois in 1940, has a special place in boomers' hearts — which is not all that surprising, considering a nostalgic burger-and-Blizzard combo is about as classic as it gets.
In a Reddit thread titled, "Why are 90% of customers elderly," a Reddit user wrote , "I've noticed that a majority of [Dairy Queen] customers are always never younger than 50." Commenters had some pretty interesting observations about this. One person wrote from their own experience, stating, "I'm almost 50 and grew up on DQ. The younger generation has more options now." Granted, 50 isn't quite a baby boomer's age (it's a little younger than the definition), but it does describe a notable sentiment.
Another commenter agreed , saying, "This. My boomer dad raised me going to Dairy Queen so it's a nostalgic thing for me, and I like the Blizzards. But better places have since opened. Also, Dairy Queen is cheaper than some of the fancier places." One Reddit user suggested a mix of things could explain baby boomers' Dairy Queen preference: "Used to be the only thing around that wasn't terrible, especially in small towns. The random group of old guys chatting over coffee was especially a thing, and yes, they had free or cheap refills too." This Reddit user also noted, "They stick with the same menu, which is familiar."
Perhaps it's because we're of a younger generation, but sometimes Dairy Queen doesn't hit the mark for us. We've previously found its soft serve to be somewhat lacking , and the beef in DQ's burgers is spongy and off-putting . But for the boomer generation, Dairy Queen is still the chain that's closest to their hearts, and if they're happy with that, then so be it.

articles.title_orig: Production suspended at Iraq's Khor Mor gas field after drone attack, sources say
articles.title_zh: Production suspended at Iraq's Khor Mor gas field after drone attack, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The Khor Mor gas field, an important energy facility, was attacked Saturday. The attack came less than 24 hours after a report that the Iranian-backed group Kataib Hezbollah had made comments about the gas facility.
In the past, Iranian-backed groups have targeted the facility. The Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq and its Kurdistan Regional Government have long asked Baghdad for drone defenses to defend the gas field and other sites. Iran has carried out more than 1,000 drone and missile attacks on the Kurdistan Region since February.
Rudaw media in Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan Region , reported that “gas production at the Khor Mor field west of Sulaimani came to a halt late Sunday after an unknown projectile struck the facility’s gas storage unit, causing significant damage, according to a Rudaw reporter on the ground.” Reports and videos online show smoke and fire billowing from the facility and the sky lit up in orange from the flames. Some reports say the facility was struck by a drone.
Rudaw added that “a source from the field confirmed the attack to Rudaw’s Peshawa Bakhtyar but couldn’t determine whether the attack came from an attack drone or a rocket, adding that the strike has caused a ‘massive fire’ in the field.”
Bakhtyar also said that the strike “hit Khor Mor’s warehouse unit, which stores nearly 1.5 thousand tons of cooking gas through 170 oil tankers. The source said the fire was close to being brought under control.” A Telegram channel linked to pro-Iran terrorist groups has said a drone was involved in the attack.
Meanwhile, on Sunday, reports noted that Abu Mujahid al-Assaf of Kataib Hezbollah had slammed Iraq’s prime minister Ali al-Zaidi and said, "we do not want to air dirty laundry in public, nor open the files of (Khor Mor) and the incitement to target it for the purpose of extorting the UAE; for whoever's house is made of glass should not throw stones at people."
The reference to Khor Mor may have been a threat. Zaidi has vowed to rein in armed groups and confiscate their weapons. Kataib Hezbollah has been in the spotlight amid this attempt to disarm various groups, including the Iranian-backed groups. Zaidi also canceled contracts at Mosul airport because the contracts were linked to “armed groups,” which is usually a euphemism for Iranian-backed terrorist groups in Iraq.
Kataib Hezbollah has targeted facilities in Iraq in the past and also targeted Saudi Arabia and killed three Americans in Jordan in January 2024. Khor Mor gas field was attacked in December 2025, February 2025 and August 2023.

Nvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) is tightening how it tracks artificial-intelligence chips sold across Southeast Asia as pressure grows on the company to prevent restricted hardware from reaching China through intermediaries.
The chipmaker now requires buyers in the region to join its fleet intelligence tracking system if they want to become official Nvidia Cloud Partners, according to TipRanks, citing Bloomberg. The program records the physical location of AI chips inside data centers.
Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Signs with NVDA.
Is NVDA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.
The incentive is meaningful.
Nvidia Cloud Partner status gives cloud companies priority access to some of Nvidia's most in-demand chips and provides a public seal of approval. Nvidia is effectively using that privilege to push more regional customers into a tracking system that had previously been voluntary.
The change comes amid mounting scrutiny from U.S. officials.
American authorities believe billions of dollars worth of restricted Nvidia chips have reached China through smuggling networks operating across Southeast Asia. In March, authorities arrested Super Micro Computer co-founder Wally Liaw on charges tied to an alleged $2.5 billion scheme to route Nvidia GPU servers into China.
Malaysia has also become a focal point. Customs authorities recently seized about $12.1 million of advanced AI chips at the country's main airport while investigating a suspected smuggling network.
Nvidia has already taken additional steps.
The company reportedly cut half of the Asian firms on its pre-approved buyer list and told cloud customers that no more than half of their Nvidia computing capacity should be rented to Chinese clients.
I think this is fundamentally a compliance-risk story rather than a demand story .
Nvidia still faces enormous demand for its chips, but the company increasingly has to prove that it knows where those chips end up.
That matters because repeated smuggling cases could give Washington justification for much tougher export restrictions, which would be far more damaging than the cost of tighter customer screening today.
The trade-off is that stricter monitoring could make Nvidia less attractive to some Southeast Asian cloud providers and complicate sales in one of the fastest-growing AI infrastructure regions.
For investors, the key things to watch are whether Washington accepts Nvidia's new controls, whether more Asian customers lose approved status, how much China-related cloud demand disappears, and whether export rules tighten further .
Nvidia is trying to solve the problem before regulators solve it for them.

articles.title_orig: Aramco Tower hit in heart of Saudi capital as Houthis launch fresh strikes
articles.title_zh: Aramco Tower hit in heart of Saudi capital as Houthis launch fresh strikes
articles.content_orig:
The Aramco Tower, a skyscraper in the Saudi Arabian capital's central financial district, had been hit by an air attack.
A statement issued via the Houthi-controlled Saba news agency confirmed the group had targeted Riyadh's business zone on Saturday, without mentioning the Aramco Tower by name.
The Saudi energy ministry said the tower had suffered only "minor damage" and no one had been killed or injured.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows more extensive damage to the building, with at least one floor appearing to have been badly hit by a missile or drone strike.
Windows on more than one level appear to have been shattered by the strike.
The Houthis also said Riyadh's airport and Aramco oil storage facilities were targeted in separate strikes. Saudi Arabia said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed several missiles.
The strikes were the latest claimed by the Yemen-based armed group against targets deep inside Saudi Arabia, which the Gulf power has struggled to contain in recent months.
It came a day after the Houthis accused a Saudi-led coalition of killing at least 33 people , including women and children, in an air strike on Yemen.
Footage broadcast by Houthi-run television channel Al Masirah showed rescuers pulling bodies from the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
Saba said 39 people had been injured in the strike. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
A Saudi-led coalition has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government, which has lost control of a large swathe of the country to the rebel group.
Although the conflict had largely been dormant in recent years, fighting has intensified following the outbreak of the Iran war.
An informal ceasefire unravelled in July after the Tehran-backed Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport Saudi Arabia said had been to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing there.
Major fighting has since resumed between Houthi forces and troops aligned with Yemen's Saudi-backed government.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects is a Chinese spy.
Huang, who heads a leading AI chipmaker and is an ally of President Donald Trump , apologized in a message to the company, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife,” according to The New York Times .
“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Nvidia announced in a press release Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Late last month, the Times reported that Huang had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center.
Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts.
“The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” Sunday’s company press release read.
“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information.”
CEO Huang supports the investigation and has agreed to cooperate with it, the board said.
There was no word of Huang’s position being in jeopardy, with the board saying it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”
Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips. It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month.
Huang, like other tech leaders, has flocked to Trump as the president embraces AI. The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September. His attendance wasn’t unusual, given that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg were also there.
